blocks.p: Sumida was two changes and two hundred and thirty yen away. Rei left the flat in the late morning, when the heat was already pressing down on the roofs, and walked to the station with his shirt sticking to his back. At the gate his card beeped and showed its balance on the little screen. He looked at the number longer than he needed to. Counting small things was what he had now instead of sleep.

The first train was cool and half empty. A woman across the aisle was knitting something small and pale yellow, her needles clicking in time with the rails. At the first change the platform was crowded with families going home for Obon, children sitting on wheeled suitcases, a father carrying a sleeping toddler and a paper bag of sweets at the same time. Rei let himself be carried along by the crowd to the next platform.

The last train was the yellow Sōbu line. It ran east, and as it crossed the long bridge over the Sumida river, everyone in the car seemed to glance out of the windows at once. The water was wide and green-brown and glittering. Pleasure boats moved slowly on it. Rei watched the river go past under the train and worked out again how many more trips the money on his card would pay for.

The man's name was Iwata. It was the same surname as the handyman in Gin's building, which meant nothing. It was a common name. He opened the door of his Sumida flat already smiling. It was the wet-eyed smile Rei had learned to dread this week. It was the smile of a person who has been carried across deep water and does not yet know that the boat is still underneath him. He was younger than the entry had made him sound, perhaps twenty-six. The flat behind him belonged to a man who had just started living again. The dishes were washed. A window was open. A photograph of someone who had died had been turned around at last, to face the room instead of the wall.

"You're his brother," Iwata said, before Rei had said anything at all, and Rei's skin went cold. He had not given this man any name. "He told me you'd come. He said you'd be tired, and that I should make you tea."

Rei sat, because standing up would have meant running. He took the tea, because refusing it would have started the conversation with an accusation. Across the low table he watched a genuinely happy man explain what had happened. Three nights ago, a soft-spoken stranger named Gin had found him at the river. Iwata had gone there to do what his grief was pushing him toward. And Gin had simply... Iwata's hands opened, helplessly grateful.
"He took the weight off," Iwata said. "He showed me how to set it down."

Iwata slept now. Iwata ate. Iwata had, he said with shining eyes, never felt so held in his life. Every true word of it went into Rei like a nail. He had come here to show this man a leash. What he had found was a man who would have died on Saturday and was alive on Tuesday. And the thing that had saved him was the thing Rei had come to destroy.

Before he could stop himself, Rei took the silver coin from his pocket and set it on the table between the cups, as if he had been emptying his pockets and forgotten it there. Iwata picked it up at once. He turned it over with real interest, read the old date, weighed it in his palm and handed it back. Nothing in him flinched. Nothing was riding him. Whatever the Healer had done here, it had not moved in. The reaction was the evidence, Gin's page said, and here the reaction was nothing at all.

Rei tried, gently, to find the seam another way. He asked whether Iwata had noticed anything he could not explain. Any debts he did not remember agreeing to. Any pull when he thought of the man who had helped him. He watched the questions slide off Iwata like rain off a raincoat. He watched the gratitude close smoothly over the place where doubt should have been. And at last he understood how it was built. The Healer did not bind people against their grief. It bound them through it. The leash was not laid on top of the wound. It was woven into the healing. To pull on the thread was to pull on the one thing holding the person together. No one could hate a hand that was also the stitches. Not Iwata. Not the widow. Not Rei.

It was not how Gin healed people. Rei knew that from the archive, from a page at the end of the chapter on suffering beings that Gin had plainly written for himself. After hard work, Gin wrote, eat. Drink water. Do something completely ordinary that needs full attention. Cooking something you actually care about, a conversation with someone you actually like. Find someone to sit with afterwards, and let ordinary things be ordinary for a while. The ordinariness is the protocol, Gin had written. Take it seriously. Gin's kind of healing sent a person back out into their own life, to their own table and their own people. The Healer's kind sent them back to the Healer.

blocks.cap: The man from Sumida refilling a cup that was still half full

blocks.p: Iwata was talking about work. He had gone back to the warehouse on Monday. His supervisor had said he looked like a new man. He laughed when he said it, a little embarrassed, and refilled Rei's cup although it was still half full. There was nothing in the flat that did not belong to an ordinary life. That was what made it unbearable.

Rei thought of the fourth rule in Gin's Grid chapter. Debt and reciprocity. When someone helps you, you help someone else. The Grid's debts were meant to move on, from one hand to the next, until nobody could say who had started it. Iwata's debt did not move. It ran in one direction only, back to the hand that had made it. And it would wait there for as long as that hand wanted.
Rei said his brother's name. He said Gin the way he had said it all through his childhood. Softly. Claiming him. The word he used to call him in from the dark.

blocks.cap: Iwata in Sumida, and the tenant still at work behind him

blocks.p: The flat changed temperature. Not Iwata. Iwata only tilted his head, still smiling, and asked if Rei was all right. It was the air that answered. The cheap fluorescent light over the sink dimmed for a breath, as if something far away had leaned its weight against a wall. And at the back of Rei's own skull, behind the two registers he kept pressed flat, he felt the thread he had reached for reach back.

It was the first time all week that the rope had had a near end as well as a far one. The Healer was on the line. Through Iwata's untouched happiness, it had just felt Rei's hand close on its work. And it was... Rei would have sworn to this, in the heat, with his pulse loud in his ears... interested.

This was the lesson the ledger could not teach him, and the man from the river just had. A knot is not a single point. A knot is a place where the rope folds back on itself, and when one end is pulled, both parts move. All week Rei had imagined himself outside the design, a reader standing over a map. In this small bright kitchen, with a saved man pouring him more tea, he finally felt what his sight had been hiding from him. The moment he touched a binding with love in his voice, he had put love into the system. The Healer kept a ledger of love the way it kept a ledger of favours. Rei had just made an entry he could not take back. It knew his frequency now. It had wanted it since the fourteenth.

He put the cup down before his hand could shake it. Across the table, Iwata's peace was undisturbed. Perfect. Sealed. That was the horror Rei would carry out of the door. The man who had been saved had felt nothing. The whole struggle had run between Rei and the thing in his brother, straight over the head of the man whose grief it was using.
He had come to Sumida to untie a knot. Instead he had proved that the rope ran both ways. That meant the Healer could be reached. It also meant the Healer could reach him.

He went back over the bridge in the hot middle of the afternoon. The car was nearly empty. An elderly couple sat side by side holding hands, saying nothing, both looking out at the river. Rei sat with the coin back in his pocket and the water going past underneath him again. He no longer knew which way the rope was moving. Was he pulling the Healer toward the light? Or was it reeling him in toward the post at Kita, one warm, patient turn at a time?
